Listen to this article Share The federal government on Tuesday said it it is looking at mobilising more than N20 billion to address issues of climate change in the North Western part of Nigeria. At a Stakeholders sumit on Climate change on Tuesday, the federal government attributed current security challenges, including food security, water, infrastructure and community stability, partly to the impact of climate change in the region. The stakeholders described the incidence of climate change as both environmental concern and development challenge with far-reaching implications for food security, water resources, public infrastructure, economic productivity and the stability of communities. “For Nigeria, and particularly for the people in the North-West region, the question is no longer whether climate change will affect our development, but how effectively we can prepare for its consequences and turn the challenge into an opportunity for sustainable growth. The stakeholders, including officials of the Ministry of Environment, the North West Development Commission NWDC, the Lagos Business School, Georgia House of Representatives and the Institute of Global Negotiation, also had investors, development partners and other stakeholders, who came together to develop a sustainable plan to confront the climat challenge. The stakeholders agreed that the problem demands well coordinated regional action. Tanko Yakasai, the Senior Special Assistant (SSA) to the President on Community Engagement (North-West), while speaking with State House journalists, outlined some of the immediate action to include proposed North West Climate Academy, Climate Investment Marketplace and Climate Fund to provide a useful framework for the effort. “Their success, however, will depend on how effectively they connect knowledge to policy, policy to investment, and investment to tangible improvements in people’s lives,” he said. “For the North-West, climate resilience is inseparable from agricultural productivity and water security.” The stakeholders while noting that the region occupies a strategic position in Nigeria’s agricultural economy, sustaining millions of people through farming, livestock production and related activities, lamented that irregular rainfall, prolonged dry spells, desertification, soil degradation and flooding threaten livelihoods and undermine economic stability, in the region. “Their consequences extend beyond affected communities, disrupting food supply chains, increasing household vulnerability and placing additional demands on public resources,” he said. ” This is the first time we’re having the a climate summit, a climate marketplace that is regional, not only in Nigeria but in the whole of Africa.” He revealed that the summit has three pillars, including the climate marketplace, where local governments, states can go into that platform and put up what they do on climate change, so that international development partners, international financial institutions, and even the local ones can see what programs they are doing on climate. ” The second one is the Climate Academy. We intend to train 10,000 youth across the northwest on climate, be it on climate resilience, be it on climate action, on anything that has to do with climate,” he added. ” Then we have the climate fund, where we source for funds so that we we tackle issues around climate change, whether flooding, whether drought, whether renewable energy, anything you think of on climate”. That fund is expected to be channeled through the office of the SSCP on community engagement to tackle those issues. “We’re looking at the region of N20 billion to say in the next four years, to help ease the problems of climate because this is what is bedeviling the whole world,” he said. The stakeholders noted that the whole world now is focused on climate change, noting that Nigeria cannot afford to ignore the crises. Mea Boykins, the Lead Consultant, described the summit as unique, adding that it represented more than a gathering of influential voices; it was an opportunity to foster strategic partnerships, mobilise investment, and advance innovative solutions to some of the most pressing climate challenges facing Northern Nigeria. “The true success of this summit will be measured not by who was in the room, but by what we accomplish together after leaving it,” Boykin said.
